meta.description: The common hybrid work schedules, what US companies actually require (2.82 office days a week on average), which days work best, and how to set one your team keeps.

coverAlt: A cream calendar with the middle three of five day tiles in navy, beside a small house with a coral roof, on a yellow background.
title: Hybrid work schedules. The common ones, and how to pick yours.
intro: A hybrid work schedule says which days people work in the office and which from home. The most common in US companies that set one is three office days a week, usually Tuesday to Thursday: the Flex Index found an average requirement of 2.82 office days a week in mid-2025, with only 7% of companies that name specific days requiring Fridays. Small companies mostly don't set days at all. What makes a schedule work is less the number of days than whether the people who work together are in on the same days, and whether the team agreed it. Every figure below links to its source. We make TinyFloor, a virtual office used by hybrid teams on their remote days, so we're not neutral on the last section.
takeaways: Among US companies with set office days, 66% require three days a week, up from 53% a year earlier, for an average of 2.82 days (Flex Index, Q2 2025).
Tuesday to Thursday are the most common office days; only 7% of companies that name specific days require Friday.
Small companies stay flexible: 70% of firms under 500 people are fully flexible (remote or employee's choice), against 12% of firms with 25,000 or more.
About 26% of paid workdays in the US were worked from home in June 2026, according to Stanford's WFH Research survey.
Gallup found teams that set their hybrid policy together are the most likely to call it fair, but only 11% of employees work under one.

sections.title: How many days a week do hybrid employees go to the office?
body: Policies have crept up, behaviour much less. The [Flex Index Q2 2025 report](https://www.lse.ac.uk/management/assets/documents/research/flex-index-reports/Flex-Report-Q2-2025.pdf), covering 8,709 US companies, found that 67% of firms have a flexible policy and 33% require full-time office attendance. Among companies with structured hybrid policies, 66% now require three days in the office, up from 53% a year earlier, for a national average of 2.82 office days a week, up from 2.49. Companies that set a minimum number of days average 2.77.

Required days rose 10% from early 2024, while actual attendance moved only 1 to 2%, based on attendance data from Stanford's Nick Bloom. Size matters most: 70% of companies with 25,000 or more employees use structured hybrid, while 70% of companies under 500 are fully flexible.

Across all workers, [Stanford's WFH Research survey](https://wfhresearch.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/WFHResearch_updates_July2026.pdf) found that about 26% of paid days in June 2026 were worked from home, and that over the past year 26% of full-time employees were hybrid, 12% fully remote and 62% fully on site. Among US employees whose jobs can be done remotely, [Gallup counted 54% hybrid](https://www.gallup.com/401384/indicator-hybrid-work.aspx) in August 2026, 25% fully remote and 21% on site.

sections.title: Which days should be office days?
body: Tuesday to Thursday, in almost every company that names days. The Flex Index found these are the most common required days, with Friday the least: only 7% of companies with specific days ask for it. Office buildings show the same shape: in the week of 27 October 2026, [Kastle's occupancy barometer](https://www.kastle.com/safety-wellness/getting-america-back-to-work/) reported Tuesday as the peak day in nearly every city it tracks.

Picking the same days as everyone else has a cost (fuller trains, booked rooms) and a benefit: the people you need are in. For a single team, the better question is which days the team most needs to be together, and that's usually the days with planning, reviews and the work that needs a whiteboard. Keep Monday and Friday for focused work, and you're back at Tuesday to Thursday.

sections.title: How to set a hybrid schedule your team will keep

items.title: Decide it with the team
items.body: Gallup found that teams that set their hybrid policy together are the most likely to say it's fair, and that as of May 2025 only 11% of employees worked under a team-set policy. A schedule handed down from above is the one people quietly bend.

items.title: Put the people who work together in on the same days
items.body: A company-wide three days doesn't help if your closest colleagues pick different ones: you commute to sit on video calls. Anchor days by team fix that.

items.title: Save office days for work that needs a room
items.body: Planning, workshops, onboarding and hard conversations go on office days; heads-down work goes on home days. A [team meeting agenda](/guides/team-meeting-agenda) that's ready beforehand makes the office day count.

items.title: Keep the meeting rules the same for everyone
items.body: If one person joins from home, everyone joins the call from their own laptop, so nobody is a voice from a speaker at the end of a table.

items.title: Review it after a month
items.body: Count who actually came in on which days. The Flex Index's gap between required and actual days suggests most schedules drift; it's better to change the rule than to have nobody follow it.

sections.title: What happens on the remote days?
body: Hybrid schedules spend a lot of thought on office days and very little on the others. On a home day, the people in the building can see who's free and turn round to ask a question; the people at home see a green dot at best, so they write a message and wait. Over time, the remote half of the week becomes the quiet half, and people at home on office days miss what's said in the room.

Two things help. First, the meeting rule above: once anyone is remote, everyone is on their own laptop. Second, somewhere the whole team can see who's around and talk without booking a call on remote days. That can be a busy chat channel, an open voice channel or a [virtual office for hybrid teams](/hybrid-teams), where everyone, at home or at a desk in the building, is on the same floor.

faq.q: What is the most common hybrid work schedule?
faq.a: Three office days a week, usually Tuesday to Thursday. The Flex Index found that 66% of US companies with structured hybrid policies require three days, for an average of 2.82 office days a week in Q2 2025.
Three days a week in the office and two at home. Most companies that use it put the office days in the middle of the week and leave Monday and Friday for home.
Set days when everyone on a team, or the whole company, is in the office together, such as Tuesday and Thursday. They make sure the people you need are there when you commute.

faq.q: How many days a week do hybrid employees go to the office?
faq.a: Companies with structured hybrid policies required 2.82 days a week on average in Q2 2025, according to the Flex Index. Attendance runs below that: required days rose 10% from early 2024 while attendance rose 1 to 2%.

faq.q: What are the best days to be in the office?
faq.a: Tuesday to Thursday for most teams: they're the most common required days, and office occupancy peaks on Tuesday. Friday is the least common office day; only 7% of companies with specific days require it.

faq.q: Who should set a hybrid schedule?
faq.a: The team that works together, within any company rule. Gallup found team-set policies are the most likely to be seen as fair, though only 11% of employees had one in May 2025.
